newsitem.title: UK: Review into British arms sales to be ready soon.
newsitem.headline: Review into British arms sales to be ready soon.

text.p: A major review of British arms sales will be ready in months and until then ministers will rule on applications to export weapons to sensitive states, a Foreign Office minister said on Monday.

Tony Lloyd said the new Labour government -- which has pledged to put human rights at the centre of foreign policy -- intended to make sure British arms could not be used for internal repression or external aggression.

Foreign Secretary Robin Cook, who regularly accused the previous Conservative government of turning a blind eye to exports of arms and material to countries such as Iraq, announced the review at the end of May.
"The review is not meant to be a lengthy one...decisions on applications (to export weapons) will be put to ministers before the review is completed," Lloyd told a seminar on arms control.

"It is not aimed at delaying things so that applications can be pushed through before the review is completed," he said, later telling journalists that it would be ready "in a matter of months, no longer."

Human rights groups say British equipment has regularly been used to suppress protests, particularly in Indonesia. Lloyd declined to speculate on whether the government would clamp down on arms sales to Jakarta.

Labour's challenge is how to balance the drive for greater human rights abroad with the interests of Britain's powerful arms industry, which employs a total of 400,000 people. Britain is one of the world's top four arms exporters.
Lloyd said the government would take a much closer look at the export of dual-use technology -- civilian equipment which can also have military applications -- and handguns.

Ministers would also pay closer attention to what happened to British arms once they were exported to make sure they were not transferred to other states. Measures would also be taken to stop Britons who took part in arms trafficking.
"What has to be at the cutting edge is the use of weapons systems. In the longer run, we are trying to influence the behaviour of those who seek to buy arms from Britain," he said.
"This is not about making the present government feel good. It's about how we can influence behaviour."

Labour wants to introduce an eight-point plan to regulate the arms industry responsibly and is also pressing for a European Union code of conduct to ensure that if Britain turns down a weapons contract, its EU partners do likewise.
Lloyd said that eventually the United States could sign up to the code.
"I don't think there is any suggestion we ought to assume we can't establish a consensus of political will at the European level and then the international level," he said.
The government also wanted to strengthen the United Nations register of conventional arms to encourage greater disclosure of information on arms exports by all countries.

"With other members of the international community, we should also explore the inclusion of other categories of weapons such as small arms, which after all are responsible for the overwhelming majority of killing on this planet," Lloyd said.
